extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, criminology, social theory, and policing studies
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying conceptual criteria for how images, common-sense beliefs, and class structures shape popular understandings and responses to crime (with emphasis on England). Useful for interpreting public discourse, press letters, and policy rhetoric about crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image of England — internal facet (core national qualities)
rubrics_metrics.description: An internal facet of the 'idea of England' relating to intrinsic national qualities believed to 'see us through' (e.g. decency, tolerance, moderation, common sense, readiness to 'rally round' in crisis). These are felt to be the culture's 'core' characteristics which appear 'in the last resort' during crises or 'finest hours'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This image functions as a unifying cultural representation that underpins appeals to normality and stability; it explains why public discourse treats certain moral/restorative responses to threats (including crime) as expressive of national character. Examples: Orwell's observations, appeals to compromise, 'bobby on the beat' ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image of England — external/imperial facet (superiority over others)
rubrics_metrics.description: An external facet forged in relation to English superiority over other nations, rooted in imperial myths and the civilizing burden narrative; produces an unspoken assumption of superiority (including working-class identification as a 'bourgeois proletariat').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This imperial image supplies content for national pride and xenophobic hierarchies in popular discourse about crime and 'outsiders'. It colors perceptions of immigrants and colonised peoples and can subtly justify differential treatment or moralising about certain groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law as ambivalent institution and ultimate recourse
rubrics_metrics.description: The law appears as a profoundly ambiguous connecting image: self-regulatory social practices are primary, but when they fail the law is the 'only arbitrator between freedom and anarchy' and is summoned in defence of national images 'in the last instance'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law serves both as necessary support for local codes and as unnecessary interference; its legitimacy is highest when local/internal controls collapse and it can be mobilised to restore the 'way of life'. This ambivalence explains contradictory popular attitudes toward police (respect for 'bobby on the beat' vs. 'all coppers are bastards').

rubrics_metrics.name: Working‑class code vs formal law (different moral logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Working-class 'code' contains norms that do not perfectly parallel legal definitions (e.g. theft from work or 'fiddles' may be acceptable, domestic violence may be treated as 'private', certain victims are seen as 'proper' victims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand crime evaluations by mapping which actions fall within community-sanctioned exceptions and which breach the code; law can be summoned against breaches of the code but is also denounced as 'interfering busybodies'. Examples: distinctions by victim, tolerance of internal theft as redressing economic balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime as central element of English ideology (mobilising force)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime is inserted at the centre of the conception of 'Englishness' as the inverse of normality and rightness; it becomes an 'evil' that threatens the balanced stabilities of the 'way of life' and therefore a powerful object for rallying support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political and media campaigns portray crime not as abstract but as a tangible threat to everyday stability; this makes moral indignation politically useful for dominant classes to create a false unity across different social conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to common sense/personal experience over theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular discourse privileges 'primary experience' and 'common sense' as superior to theory or expert analysis; claims grounded in everyday experience (or appeals to it) are seen as more legitimate and 'real'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In interpreting public opinion (e.g., letters to editors), treat appeals to anecdote and direct experience as rhetorical authority rather than as objective evidence. Note editors' valuation of such testimony even when it lacks concrete detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditionalism and empiricism fused in English ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: English ruling-class ideology is diffused in a miasma of 'traditionalism' and 'empiricism': traditionalism derives the present from the past, empiricism ties the future to the present, producing a legitimating system that privileges the concrete and practical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fusion helps explain resistance to theoretical critique and the elevation of 'how things are' as normative; when analysing discourse, look for arguments that naturalise social arrangements via appeal to historical continuity and 'practical' experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: English anti‑intellectualism (suspicion of theorists)
rubrics_metrics.description: A cultural tendency to devalue intellectuals and 'theorisers' who are depicted as out of touch with 'real life'; this stance is partly a class response to unequal distribution of validated knowledge (certificates, degrees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate populist dismissal of expert-led explanations of crime; public arguments will often frame policy debate as 'cut the talking and listen to someone who really knows' (i.e., lived experience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Us/Them corporate class consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Working-class culture organizes social life in a strong 'us' (community, solidarity) versus 'them' (authorities, employers) structure; this produces both solidarity and deferential acceptance of containment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This corporate form of consciousness yields context-specific moral judgements and can produce contradictory positions (e.g., endorsing national ruling ideas in general but resisting them in situated practice). It grounds many working-class moral responses to crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common sense as fragmentary, unexamined, and accommodating
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense is a chaotic aggregate of disparate, fragmentary conceptions—largely unexamined maxims and prejudices—that do not test internal coherence and often absorb sedimented elements of earlier ideologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing popular belief, expect contradictions and 'pragmatic acceptance' rather than coherent counter-ideologies; common sense often 'tags' new facts onto existing frameworks without challenging deeper structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate versus hegemonic culture and pragmatic acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Subordinate (corporate) cultures negotiate and qualify hegemonic ideas, producing pragmatic acceptance: subordinate attitudes are different yet remain bounded by ruling ideas, enabling cross-class alliances and preserving hegemony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret public support for ostensibly hegemonic positions (e.g., tough on crime) as negotiated and context-dependent rather than as wholehearted ideological conversion; look for situational exceptions that maintain subordinate autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personal testimony in media and public debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters to editors and press discourse frequently invoke personal testimony, often indirectly, to lend weight to opinions about crime (e.g., 'working-class mother of three' signatures, hypothetical appeals to suffering a crime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such testimonies as rhetorical devices that elevate common-sense authority; note that many such appeals are not concrete accounts but function to authenticate viewpoints in public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social anxiety as driver of conservative moral indignation about crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific historical social changes (outlined later in the text) interact with traditional ideological resources to produce strong conservative moral responses to crime, mobilising public fear and demand for control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In explanations of rising punitive sentiment, consider both long-standing cultural frames (common sense, images of England) and contingent structural changes that create social anxiety; do not treat moral panic as arising solely from objective crime increases.
